_timing: No narration yet. Each beat is the larger of the time it needs to finish animating and the time it takes to read, plus a 22-frame hold. This is a floor, not considered pacing — measure a real read and switch this topic to voiceCuts.

beats.note: The man who invented it calls that a distortion. 'The iconic 25-minute sessions,' Francesco Cirillo writes, 'aren't the technique. They're just one expression of it.'

beats.name: Francesco Cirillo
beats.role: A university student who could not concentrate, timing himself with the first thing to hand on the kitchen counter: a wind-up timer shaped like a tomato. Pomodoro is simply Italian for tomato.

beats.lead: The first challenge he set himself
beats.note: 'Can I study for just two minutes without interruption?' The famous 25 came later, and even that, he says, is one expression of the method, not the point of it.

beats.lead: Ask him how many pomodoros to aim for
beats.text: His answer: even none is fine.
beats.note: 'Your goal isn't to complete Pomodoros,' he says, 'it's to become aware of what happens in your mind.' A focus method whose own author does not care how much you get done.

beats.line: The tomato is a timer, not a target.
